title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) for Intent→Configuration NetOps: Null Results on a Synthetic Verifier-Checked Task Bank
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment testing whether a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) reduces verifier-detected semantic invariant violations for intent→device-configuration translation. Design: public synthetic NetOps task bank, N=240 paired tasks, gpt-5-mini generator, deterministic pybatfish-style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), one shared initial generation per task reused across arms (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate), and at most one bounded repair attempt per task. Results (artifact-backed): every generated candidate satisfied the verifier in both arms (n11 = 240; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), yielding paired estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The prespecified secondary primary comparison (GVR vs schema-constrained baseline, C vs B) listed in the preregistration was not executed in the archived run and no recorded rationale appears in the execution artifacts; we state this explicitly. Interpretation: under the executed shared-generation semantics and this synthetic workload, bounded GVR provided no verifier-detectable benefit because there were no verifier-detectable errors to correct. We document the preregistration→execution deviation that invalidates the preregistered power assumption (independent per-condition generation vs executed shared generation), enumerate threats to inference, and give artifact-grounded recommendations (independent per-condition generation, adversarial/golden injections, multi-model runs, expanded verifier coverage).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→device-configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency but raises safety concerns: stochastic generators can emit syntactically plausible yet semantically incorrect commands that violate network invariants (reachability, workflow order, or access-control predicates). Prior systems and surveys therefore recommend architectures that interpose deterministic validators and iterative repair (generate–verify–repair, GVR) to detect and correct mechanically checkable defects prior to execution. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment (study_id: c1_gvr_semantic_eval_prereg_v1) to test the specific operational question: does inserting a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop reduce verifier-detected semantic invariant violations relative to an unconstrained baseline when evaluated on a synthetic NetOps task bank? The run, analysis, and artifacts are archived and authoritative (preregistration_sha256: eaedeae9aa302327e090d519a7a16f514d7fb79a472071aaf171f2f618c8ad4d). Our contributions: (1) a fully preregistered, artifact-backed paired evaluation on N=240 tasks using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (2) transparent execution accounting showing shared-initial-candidate semantics produced one generation per task reused across arms (model_calls_used = 240) and that every generation satisfied the verifier (n11 = 240); (3) confirmatory statistics and an explicit reconciliation of preregistered power assumptions with executed semantics; (4) artifact-grounded operational recommendations to restore discordance potential and adversarial sensitivity.
sections.related_work: Three strands most closely relate to this study. (i) LLM failure modes for code and structured outputs: surveys and case studies document hallucinations and fabricated outputs for code and operational artifacts, motivating deterministic validators in production NetOps pipelines. (ii) Generate–Verify–Repair and constrained-decoding methods: prior work shows generate–verify–repair architectures and grammar/schema-constrained decoding reduce surface-level failures (syntax, executable artifacts) but often evaluate syntactic or compilation properties rather than domain-specific semantic invariants. (iii) NetOps verification and intent-translation literature: NetOps research emphasizes verifier-driven evaluation (reachability and policy invariants), intent-based translators, and operator-in-the-loop governance for high-stakes changes. Our run differs by being preregistered, paired, and analysis-executor–frozen (paired_binary_analysis_v1), and by reporting an artifact-backed null outcome that directly demonstrates how evaluation semantics (shared vs independent generation) condition measurable GVR benefit.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (paired difference in verifier-detected semantic-violation rate). The preregistration specified two prespecified primary comparisons (C vs A and C vs B) with Bonferroni correction (family alpha = 0.05 → per-comparison alpha = 0.025) and froze the analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1. Execution contract (frozen): task bank = public synthetic NetOps task bank (12 clusters × 20 tasks = 240 tasks); requested model = gpt-5-mini; deterministic verifier = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; maximum_model_calls = 480; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. Crucial executed semantics (recorded in the archived manifest): generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1. Consequence: each task used a single shared generation reused across both arms; model_calls_used = 240 (shared-generation). Analysis settings: paired_binary_analysis_v1 (exact McNemar two-sided test and paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI, bootstrap_resamples = 10,000, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Missingness and exclusions: preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' rules applied; execution manifest records planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, failed_episode_count = 0. Important prespecified-but-unexecuted item: the preregistration listed (C vs B) (GVR vs schema-constrained baseline) as a prespecified primary comparison. The archived execution artifacts document that this prespecified comparison was not executed; we explicitly state that no recorded rationale for the omission appears in the archived run.
sections.results: Execution accounting (artifact-backed): planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480; model_calls_used = 240 under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Contingency table observed by the preregistered analysis executor: n11 = 240 (both arms accepted), n10 = 0 (guarded-only), n01 = 0 (baseline-only), n00 = 0 (both rejected). Rates: baseline_success_rate = 1.0; guarded_success_rate = 1.0; paired estimate = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00. Paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Repair usage: for every episode validator trace shows repair_applied = false; the bounded repair loop never executed because the shared initial candidate satisfied validator predicates for every task. Statistical degeneracy and causal explanation: zero discordant pairs render the paired estimator degenerate—no within-pair disagreements exist to estimate a differential effect. The observed p-value (1.00) and the collapsed bootstrap CI are deterministic consequences of the contingency under the preregistered analysis executor. This degeneracy is causally linked to two artifact-supported mechanisms: (1) task/verifier alignment—the synthetic task bank combined with the chosen prompt/generator produced verifier-acceptable candidates across all tasks; (2) evaluation semantics—shared_initial_candidate eliminated independent per-condition stochastic variation, removing discordance potential and invalidating the preregistered power assumption that assumed independent per-condition generation.
sections.discussion: Conservative interpretation: under the executed shared-generation semantics and the supplied synthetic workload/verifier, bounded GVR added no verifier-detectable value because there were no verifier-detectable errors to correct. This is an artifact-supported null result, not evidence that GVR cannot help under other plausible evaluation semantics. Implications for evaluation practice: to measure GVR’s effectiveness under generator stochasticity, evaluations must permit independent per-condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true), inject adversarial or golden-reference tasks that reliably trigger verifier failures, or test multiple generator families and prompt variants. The preregistration contained these design elements as options (golden injections, independent generation) but the archived run executed shared-generation semantics and omitted the prespecified C vs B comparison; both facts alter inferential strength. Threats to validity: internal validity is limited by the preregistration→execution mismatch (power assumption invalidated by shared generation); construct validity is limited by verifier completeness (passing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 does not guarantee absence of all operational risk); external validity is limited by a single model (gpt-5-mini), a synthetic task bank, and a single bounded repair budget. Recommendations (artifact-grounded): re-run with independent per-condition generation using the archived task manifest and RNG seeds; inject adversarial/golden tasks; run multiple generator models; increase repair budget and record repair-iteration distributions; broaden verifier invariants or integrate formal/SMT-based checks to reduce oracle incompleteness.
sections.conclusion: A fully preregistered, artifact-archived paired experiment found that under executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and the supplied synthetic NetOps task bank, every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic verifier in both arms (n11 = 240), producing a degenerate null paired estimate (0.0), exact McNemar p = 1.00, and bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The archived run did not execute a prespecified primary comparison (GVR vs schema-constrained baseline, C vs B) and the shared-generation semantics invalidated the preregistered power assumption that assumed independent per-condition generation; both are declared and discussed as preregistration→execution deviations. We publish the authoritative artifacts so others can reproduce the accounting and re-execute the preregistered independent-generation design, adversarial injections, and multi-model comparisons required to more robustly evaluate GVR’s operational value.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and verifier scope: N = 240 tasks were synthetic and evaluated against a pybatfish-style deterministic validator; results may not generalize to production topologies, vendor-specific syntax, or semantic invariants not encoded in the verifier.

Shared-generation semantics: the archived run used generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial generation per task reused across arms). This design reduced model-call cost but removed per-arm stochastic variation and therefore removed sensitivity to detect GVR benefits that rely on independent per-condition generator variability; the preregistered power calculation assumed independent per-condition generation and therefore does not apply to the executed design.
Single-model evaluation: the experiment used one generator (gpt-5-mini); cross-model generality is not established.
Repair budget: only a single bounded repair iteration was permitted; different or larger repair budgets or iterative strategies might produce different outcomes.
Verifier completeness risk: passing the deterministic verifier does not guarantee absence of all operational risks (unobserved invariants or properties outside the verifier model).

Prespecified comparison not executed: the preregistration included a prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison (C vs B) that was not executed in the archived run; the artifacts do not record a rationale, which is an unresolved procedural limitation.
